title: Narrative tenses
tagline: Four past tenses working together to tell a story with a clear order of events.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze
why: A good B2 story doesn't just use the past simple. Setting the scene, showing what was already happening, and stepping further back to explain what came before all need different past tenses working together — and Writing Part 2's story task rewards exactly that control.

diagrams.title: Four layers of one story

marks.label: The team had already trained for months.
It was raining and the crowd was arriving.
The whistle blew and the match started.

diagrams.caption: By the time the whistle blew, the team had trained for months, and the crowd was still arriving.

rows.label: Past simple
cells: the main events, one after another

rows.label: Past continuous
cells: the background scene, or an action interrupted

rows.label: Past perfect simple
cells: something finished before the main story time

rows.label: Past perfect continuous
cells: an activity going on before that point, often explaining a result

diagrams.title: Interrupting a background action
diagrams.caption: The longer background action is continuous; the short event that cuts across it is simple.

head: Tense
Form
Job
Example
rows: She opened the door and stepped outside.
the scene, or a longer action in progress
It was pouring with rain and the wind was howling.
an action cut short by a sudden event
We were queuing for tickets when the alarm went off.
a completed event before the story time
By the time we arrived, the film had already started.
an activity going on before that point, often with a result
Her hands were shaking because she had been climbing for an hour.
when / while / as / after / before / by the time
As soon as the bell rang, everyone rushed outside.

use.point: Setting the scene with the past continuous

examples.text: The market was buzzing with tourists, and vendors were shouting out their prices.
Nadia was walking home from rehearsal when she heard the news.

use.point: Main events, one after another, in the past simple

examples.text: Mateo grabbed his bag, ran for the bus and just caught it.
Miss Vega opened the envelope and read the results out loud.

use.point: Going further back with the past perfect

examples.text: By the time the band came on stage, half the crowd had already left.
examples.note: finished before the main story time

examples.text: Liam realised he had left his phone on the bus.
examples.note: past perfect after a reporting verb

examples.text: Sofia was exhausted because she had been rehearsing since six that morning.
examples.note: an activity, not just a fact — past perfect continuous

use.point: Linking the layers with time words

examples.text: As soon as the rain stopped, the match started again.
examples.note: as soon as + past simple, past simple

examples.text: While Mateo was setting up the equipment, Sofia checked the microphones.
By the time she had finished explaining, the whole class understood.

watch_out.wrong: When I arrived, they were already leaving five minutes before.
watch_out.right: When I arrived, they had already left five minutes before.
watch_out.why: An event completed before another past event needs the past perfect, not the past continuous.

watch_out.wrong: While I walked to school, it started to rain.
watch_out.right: While I was walking to school, it started to rain.
watch_out.why: The longer background action after while is usually continuous, not simple.

watch_out.wrong: She was living in Cusco for two years before she moved to Lima.
watch_out.right: She had lived in Cusco for two years before she moved to Lima.
watch_out.why: A finished period before another past event needs the past perfect, not the past continuous.

watch_out.wrong: I was knowing him for years before we became friends.
watch_out.right: I had known him for years before we became friends.
watch_out.why: State verbs don't take the continuous — even in a narrative, use the past perfect simple.

watch_out.wrong: By the time the bell rang, we finished the test.
watch_out.right: By the time the bell rang, we had finished the test.
watch_out.why: By the time + a past event needs the past perfect for the earlier action.

dialogue.title: The blackout
dialogue.context: Liam is telling Sofia and Mateo what happened during last night's power cut at his house.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: So I was doing my homework when suddenly all the lights went out.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: No way. What had happened before that — did you already know there was a problem?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Actually, yes. The neighbours had mentioned some work on the street earlier that day.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: So while you were sitting there in the dark, what did you do?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I found a candle. My hands were shaking a bit because I had been reading a horror story just before.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Of course you were reading a horror story. Then what?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: My sister came downstairs — she had been sleeping and the noise woke her up.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: By the time the power came back, how long had you two been sitting there?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: About an hour. We had told each other every scary story we knew.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: That explains why you looked so tired this morning.

items.sentence: The sun ___ and the birds were singing when we set off.
By the time Mateo arrived, the meeting ___.
items.why: finished before another past event → past perfect

items.sentence: While Nadia ___ dinner, the phone rang three times.
items.why: longer background action interrupted → past continuous

items.sentence: Sofia was out of breath because she ___ for the bus.
items.why: an activity before the story moment, explaining a result → past perfect continuous

items.sentence: We ___ the museum, and then we walked to the café.
items.why: one main event in the sequence → past simple

items.sentence: I knew the town well because I ___ there as a child.
items.why: an earlier, finished period before another past state → past perfect

items.sentence: As soon as the teacher ___, everyone stopped talking.
items.why: a quick event that triggers the next → past simple

items.sentence: It ___ heavily, so we decided to stay inside.
items.why: ongoing weather forming the background → past continuous

summary: Past simple carries the main events, one after another.
Past continuous paints the background scene or a longer action that gets interrupted.
Past perfect (simple or continuous) reaches further back, before the main story time.
Signal words — when, while, as, by the time, as soon as — tell you which tense to expect.
In a story, mixing all four tenses on purpose is what makes it read like a real account, not a list of events.
